Key

This key contains relevant variables to our analysis and their units of measurement:

1. Average Water Speed (cm/s)

2. Average Water Direction (degrees)

3. Chlorophyll (ug/L)

4. Temperature (°C)

5. Dissolved Oxygen (mg/L)

6. Dissolved Oxygen (% Saturation)

7. pH

8. Salinity (ppm)

9. Specific Conductance (mS/cm)

10. Turbidity (Formazin Nephelometric Units (FNU))

Introduction

This project examines a dataset provided by the Queensland Government Open Data Portal containing measurements of water physicochemcical parameters of the Brisbane River in Australia (Fedorov). The dataset includes timestamps, record numbers, and various characteristics of the river during a given instance. Using this data, we aim to test whether or not the average water speed is influenced by these river characteristics. Understanding water speed is crucial because it affects numerous things: river habitats and aquatic biodiversity, agriculture, hydroelectric power generation, erosion, flood risk management, and many others. Monitoring these speeds is tantamount to ensuring risk management and environmental protection (Fain).

Section 1: Descriptive Statistics and Checking Assumptions 

We begin our analysis by first examining some characteristics of the dataset. Descriptive statistics are helpful in arming us with useful data points as well as allowing us to detect potential outliers whether that be highly correlated variables or null values (NA). We will ignore columns Timestamp column as it may over complicate our analysis and the various [quality] columns due to their long stretch of null values. 

water <- df %>% 
  select(`Average Water Speed`, `Average Water Direction`, Chlorophyll, Temperature, `Dissolved Oxygen`, pH, Salinity, `Specific Conductance`, Turbidity)
water

This dataset contains over 30,000 observations of the Brisbane River, capturing variation in the water’s physicochemical parameters across 30-minute intervals. Before cleaning, many variables contained a substantial amount of missing values, most notably temperature (5164 missing), dissolved oxygen (4300 missing), salinity (3958 missing), and turbidity (2000 missing). After removing these rows to ensure we only have complete observations, the dataset retained the majority of its observations while dropping potential inconsistencies. (Potentially revise to fill the missing with avg or median values, depends on the gap lengths*)

clean_water <- na.omit(water)
#Uncleaned and cleaned placeholders
water_plot <- water %>% 
  select(`Average Water Speed`) %>% 
           mutate(stage = "Before Cleaning")
clean_water_plot <- clean_water %>% 
  select(`Average Water Speed`) %>% 
  mutate(stage = "After Cleaning")

combined <- bind_rows(water_plot, clean_water_plot)

combined$stage <- factor(combined$stage, levels = c("Before Cleaning", "After Cleaning"))

ggplot(combined, aes(x = `Average Water Speed`)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth=2, fill="blue", color="white") + 
  facet_wrap(~stage) +
  labs(title = "Distribtuon of Average",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Average Water Speed (cm/s)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
## Warning: Removed 20 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_bin()`).

ggsave("figures/water_speed_distribution.png", 
       plot = last_plot(),  # or replace with your saved plot object, e.g. speed_plot
       width = 8, height = 5, dpi = 300)
## Warning: Removed 20 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_bin()`).

Comparing the summary statistics before and after cleaning the data, some key trends slightly shifted, reflecting the removal of those null/extreme values. For instance, the mean average water speed decreased from ~16.80 to ~16.01, and the median from ~13.39 to ~12.33; the range remained wide, indicating some persistent extreme values. With regards to the other average water direction and the physicochemical parameters, they also exhibited minor changes. (Weighted regression will allow us to skip z-score scaling)

Overall, the removal of these missing values slightly adjusted the descriptive statistics, retaining variability and the general patterns of the dataset. This version provides us with a more reliable starting point for further analysis.

Section 2: Model Preparation and Fitting

Here, we are interested in seeing if there are any variables with relationships that are a bit too strong. Highly correlated pairs can lead to multicollinearity, which can inflate standard errors and lower our model’s estimates and predicting power. On a 0 to 1 scale, a common “rule-of-thumb” threshold is usually <0.7, with any pairs going past this potentially indicating multicollinearity. As shown below, Salinity and Specific Conductance are extremely correlated (~0.999), which makes sense logically as conductance of water is highly dependent on its salt contents so if a river is measured to have a high amount of salinity, its specific conductance will also be high. To address this, we will remove Specific Conductance from our model, retaining Salinity as its presenter. 

cor(clean_water[,-c(1,9)])
##                         Average Water Direction  Chlorophyll Temperature
## Average Water Direction             1.000000000 -0.005431517 -0.06152078

## Dissolved Oxygen                   -0.016341960  0.214485051 -0.42673370
## pH                                  0.054432136 -0.115725922 -0.58335925
## Salinity                           -0.016974558 -0.230532217 -0.12532087
## Specific Conductance               -0.017439909 -0.230784434 -0.10682186
##                         Dissolved Oxygen          pH    Salinity

## Temperature                  -0.42673370 -0.58335925 -0.12532087

predictors <- clean_water %>% 
  select(`Average Water Direction`, Chlorophyll, Temperature, `Dissolved Oxygen`, pH, Salinity, `Specific Conductance`, Turbidity)
corr_matrix <- cor(predictors)

corr_plot <- ggcorrplot(corr_matrix, method = "square",
           type = "lower",
           lab = TRUE,
           lab_size = 3,
           colors = c("red", "white", "steelblue"),
           title = "Correlation Matrix of Physicochemical Predictors",
           ggtheme = theme_minimal()) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=45, hjust=1)) + 
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.65))
corr_plot

ggsave("figures/correlation_heatmap_before.png", plot = corr_plot, width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 300)

After we removed Specific Conductance, no pair of variables exceeded the 0.7 threshold anymore. 

cor(clean_water[,c(1,8)])
##                      Average Water Speed Specific Conductance
## Average Water Speed            1.0000000           -0.2196674
## Specific Conductance          -0.2196674            1.0000000
predictors_cleaned <- clean_water %>% 
  select(`Average Water Direction`, Chlorophyll, Temperature, `Dissolved Oxygen`, pH, Salinity, Turbidity)
corr_matrix <- cor(predictors_cleaned)

corr_plot <- ggcorrplot(corr_matrix, method = "square",
           type = "lower",
           lab = TRUE,
           lab_size = 3,
           colors = c("red", "white", "steelblue"),
           title = "Correlation Matrix of Physicochemical Predictors (Omitted Conductance)",
           ggtheme = theme_minimal()) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle=45, hjust=1)) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.65))
corr_plot

ggsave("figures/correlation_heatmap_after.png", 
       plot = corr_plot, 
       width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 300)

We create a multiple linear regression model with Average Water Speed being our response variable and the remaining variables (Average Water Direction, Chlorophyll, Temperature, Dissolved Oxygen, pH, Salinity, Turbidity) as our predictors. We will approach this using manual selection, later using step-wise selection to assess if they align. 

Looking at the output, we notice that the p-values for Average Water Direction (0.0971) and Temperature (p = 0.5361) exceeds the 0.05 significance threshold, indicating that they may not significantly affect/predict average water direction; we will consider removing temperature first and refitting.

model <- lm(`Average Water Speed` ~ `Average Water Direction` + Chlorophyll+Temperature+`Dissolved Oxygen`+pH+Salinity+Turbidity, data=clean_water) 
summary(model)

Upon refitting, Average Water Direction’s p-value (0.0893) still exceeds the 0.05 threshold so we will remove it and refit once more.

model2 <- lm(`Average Water Speed` ~ `Average Water Direction` + Chlorophyll+`Dissolved Oxygen`+pH+Salinity+Turbidity, data=clean_water) 
summary(model2)

The tentative final model includes Chlorophyll, Dissolved Oxygen, pH, Salinity, and Turbidity. Temperature and Average Water Direction were excluded due to lack of significance. When using stepwise selection using Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) penalty (since it scales with sample size), it resulted in the same model, indicating that this model provides a balance between goodness of fit and model complexity. 

The adjusted R^2 of 0.137 indicates that our model explains a moderate portion of variation in average water speed. Much of the remaining variability is likely driven by environmental factors not captured in this dataset. Regardless, our predictors’ statistical significance do prove that they truly have an effect on determining average water speed, even if the model doesn’t explain most of the variation. Rivers are inherently dynamic, as their flow can be strongly affected by a variety of external forces and conditions (Trent and Brown).

full_model <- lm(`Average Water Speed`~Chlorophyll+`Dissolved Oxygen`+pH+Salinity+Turbidity, data=clean_water)
summary(full_model)

Furthermore, the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) values for all predictors are well below the common threshold of 5, indicating that multicollinearity is not a concern of this model.

vif(full_model)
##        Chlorophyll `Dissolved Oxygen`                 pH           Salinity 
##           1.150727           1.347967           1.330623           1.117600 
##          Turbidity 
##           1.077958

Section 3: Diagnostics

In order to ensure the assumptions of our linear regression model are met, several diagnostic checks were performed. We are looking to confirm if the assumptions of linearity, constant variance, and normality of residuals are satisfied. The fitted values versus residuals was plotted to visually show if any patterns are recognized and we see that there is this downward, fanning of the point suggesting possible heteroscedasticity. The Breusch-Pagan Test (BP) yielded an extremely small p- value (<2.2e-16), undeniably rejecting the null hypothesis of constant variance, confirming our suspicion of heteroscedasticity. 

resid_df <- data.frame(fitted = full_model$fitted.values,
                       residuals = full_model$residuals)

resid_plot <- ggplot(resid_df, aes(x=fitted, y=residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha=0.4, color="steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, color="firebrick", linetype="dashed") +
  labs(title="Residuals vs. Fitted Values",
       x="Fitted Values",
       y="Residuals") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5))

Our Q-Q plot shows a slightly exponential trend beginning to form about x-axis = 1, causing some deviation in our linearity assumption. Our Component + Residuals (crPlots) also agree with this deviation of linearity, indicating that some transformation may be necessary. 

qq_plot <- ggplot(resid_df, aes(sample=residuals)) +
    stat_qq(color="steelblue", alpha=0.5) +
    stat_qq_line(color="firebrick", linetype="dashed") +
    labs(title="Normal Q-Q Plot",
         x="Theoretical Quantiles",
         y="Sample Quantiles") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust=0.5))
qq_plot

ggsave("figures/qq_plot.png", 
       plot = qq_plot, 
       width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 300)
crPlots(full_model)

cook <- cooks.distance(full_model)
max(cook)
## [1] 0.008554348

A Box-Cox transformation was performed to determine whether a power transformation to the response would improve model assumptions of linearity. The analysis suggested that the optimal lambda value is 1, indicating that no transformation is necessary. Therefore, the response variable is retained on its original scale.

box_cox <- powerTransform(`Average Water Speed` ~Chlorophyll+`Dissolved Oxygen` +pH+Salinity+Turbidity, data=clean_water) 
summary(box_cox) 
## bcPower Transformation to Normality 
##    Est Power Rounded Pwr Wald Lwr Bnd Wald Upr Bnd
## Y1    0.2065        0.21       0.1937       0.2192
## 
## Likelihood ratio test that transformation parameter is equal to 0
##  (log transformation)
##                            LRT df       pval
## LR test, lambda = (0) 1089.636  1 < 2.22e-16
## 
## Likelihood ratio test that no transformation is needed
##                            LRT df       pval
## LR test, lambda = (1) 11736.15  1 < 2.22e-16

To address the issue of heteroscedasticity, we apply the Weighted Least Squares (WLS) to give less influence to observations with higher variance in residuals, resulting in more reliable coefficient estimates and improving the homoscedasticity assumption. 

ols <- lm(`Average Water Speed` ~Chlorophyll+`Dissolved Oxygen` +pH+Salinity+Turbidity, data=clean_water)
residual_sq <- resid(ols)^2
var_model <- lm(residual_sq~fitted(ols))
pred_var <- predict(var_model)
weight <- (1/pred_var)
wls <- lm(`Average Water Speed` ~Chlorophyll+`Dissolved Oxygen` +pH+Salinity+Turbidity, data=clean_water, weights=weight)
summary(wls)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = `Average Water Speed` ~ Chlorophyll + `Dissolved Oxygen` + 
##     pH + Salinity + Turbidity, data = clean_water, weights = weight)
## 
## Weighted Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -1.7642 -0.6869 -0.2600  0.4204  8.2802 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                      Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)        -227.51740    8.79744 -25.862  < 2e-16 ***
## Chlorophyll          -0.14242    0.04801  -2.967  0.00301 ** 
## `Dissolved Oxygen`   -4.88709    0.14930 -32.733  < 2e-16 ***
## pH                   37.72614    1.13579  33.216  < 2e-16 ***
## Salinity             -0.96587    0.02375 -40.666  < 2e-16 ***
## Turbidity             0.25246    0.02245  11.246  < 2e-16 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.9994 on 20022 degrees of freedom
## Multiple R-squared:  0.1653, Adjusted R-squared:  0.1651 
## F-statistic: 793.2 on 5 and 20022 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

Since applying the WLS approach, the BP test yielded a higher p-value (0.000204), indicating that while some heteroscedasticity remains, the variance of residuals has improved compared to the original model. 

bptest(wls)
## 
##  studentized Breusch-Pagan test
## 
## data:  wls
## BP = 24.141, df = 5, p-value = 0.000204

Using the outlier test, we identified 10 observations with unusually high average water speeds that are extreme compared to the rest of the dataset. These values have the potential to unduly influence the regression results so we will remove them in an effort to improve model reliability. 

outlierTest(wls)

## 5051  5.978047         2.2966e-09   4.5996e-05

outlier <- c(1,2,3340,3805,4104,3385,3524,3746,3938,5051,11844)
clean_water[outlier,]

final <- clean_water[!(seq_len(nrow(clean_water)) %in% outlier), ]
final
## # A tibble: 20,017 × 9

##                    <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
##  1                 1.26                      157.         1.62        20.0

## # ℹ 5 more variables: `Dissolved Oxygen` <dbl>, pH <dbl>, Salinity <dbl>,
## #   `Specific Conductance` <dbl>, Turbidity <dbl>
final_ols <- lm(`Average Water Speed` ~Chlorophyll+`Dissolved Oxygen` +pH+Salinity+Turbidity, data=final)
residual_sq <- resid(final_ols)^2
var_model<-lm(residual_sq~fitted(final_ols))
pred_var<- predict(var_model)
final_weight <- (1/pred_var)

After refitting the final model, including the weight, the model still exhibits heteroscedasticity as it still fails to reject the BP test’s null hypothesis. However, the weighted residuals indicate that heteroscedasticity has been reduced once more, reflected by the higher p-value (p ~ 0.00011) compared to the original (<2.2e-16) and prior (0. 

final_wls <- lm(`Average Water Speed` ~Chlorophyll+`Dissolved Oxygen` +pH+Salinity+Turbidity, data=final, weights=final_weight)
bptest(final_wls)
## 
##  studentized Breusch-Pagan test
## 
## data:  final_wls
## BP = 25.424, df = 5, p-value = 0.0001154

Section 4: Predictive Validation

In order to assess whether or not the model generalizes beyond the data it was fit on, we implement a train/test split approach into a 80% and 20% subset, respectively. The weighted least squares model was refit using only the training data, with weights recalculated with training residuals to avoid overlap with the test set. The fitted model was then used to predict Average Water Speed.

#randomizing seed for reproducibility + 7 is lucky
set.seed(777)

#Split
split <- sample.split(final$`Average Water Speed`, SplitRatio = 0.8)

#Train/Test sets
training_set <- subset(final, split == TRUE)
test_set <- subset(final, split == FALSE)

#Refit WLS on training data only
train_ols <- lm(`Average Water Speed`~Chlorophyll+`Dissolved Oxygen`+pH+Salinity+Turbidity, data=training_set)
train_resid_sq <- resid(train_ols)^2
train_var_model <- lm(train_resid_sq~fitted(train_ols))
train_pred_var <- predict(train_var_model)
train_weight <- 1/train_pred_var
train_wls <- lm(`Average Water Speed`~Chlorophyll+`Dissolved Oxygen`+pH+Salinity+Turbidity, data=training_set, weights=train_weight)
summary(train_wls)

The resulting test set RMSE was 12.02 cm/s and MAE was 8.98 cm/s. The RMSE aligns closely with the residual standard error of the original unweighted model (~12.08 cm/s), suggesting that the model’s predictive performance on unseen data is consistent with its in sample fit rather than reflecting overfitting.

Section 5: Analysis

The final weighted least squares model depicts how Chlorophyll, Dissolved Oxygen, pH, Salinity, and Turbidity influence the average water speed of the Brisbane River. Within the parameter estimates, all coefficients are statistically significant at the 0.01 level, indicating well-supported points. Notably, dissolved oxygen has a strong negative effect (Estimate ~ -4.91), suggesting that higher oxygen levels are correlated with lower water speeds. pH displays a very strong, positive effect (Estimate 37.73), implying higher pH associates with faster water speeds. Salinity has a moderately negative effect (Estimate ~ -0.97), while Turbidity (Estimate~ 0.25) and Chlorophyll (Estimate~ -0.15) produced smaller but still significant effects. The model explains roughly 17.4% of variability in water speed, suggesting that other environmental factors not included within the dataset likely contribute to variation. 

summary(final_wls)

Section 6: Limitations and Future Implementations

While the final model provides statistically significant and interpretable relationships between physiochemical parameters and average water speed, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the model explains only a modest portion of the variability in water speed (Adjusted R2 ≈ 0.174), suggesting that important drivers of river flow are not captured in this dataset. According to the research (Less et al. 1181), hydrological factors such as rainfall, tidal cycles, and upstream discharge volume are known to strongly influence river velocity. However, these were unavailable in the source data, and their absence likely accounts for much of the unexplained variance.

Second, the time stamp variable was excluded from modeling to simplify the analysis, meaning temporal structure such as diurnal tidal patterns or seasonal variation, was not directly incorporated. Given that river flow is inherent interdependent, future work could explore this structure directly, either through time-series methods that account for autocorrelation between sequential 30-minute readings, or through mixed-effects models that treat time-of-day or season as structured random effects.

Finally, the train/test validation performed did give us confirmation that the data generalizes well with unseen data, but this could be further extended using k-fold cross-validation to give us a greater range of estimates across many partitions to better defend our findings.

Conclusion

This analysis provides a comprehensive assessment of how key physicochemical parameters influence the average water speed of the Brisbane River. Using multiple linear regression and rigidly considering model assumptions, we identified Chlorophyll, Dissolved Oxygen, pH, Salinity, and Turbidity as significant predictors of water speed. The Weighted Least Squares approach improved the reliability of coefficient estimates by reducing the influence of heteroscedasticity, and removal of extreme outliers further strengthened model stability. While the final model explains approximately 17.4% of the variability in water speed, the statistical significance of all predictors demonstrates that these environmental factors meaningfully contribute to river flow dynamics. Notably higher Dissolved Oxygen and Salinity are associated with slower flows, whereas higher pH and Turbidity relate to faster speeds, highlighting the various complex interactions of physicochemical properties in shaping river behavior.

Overall, this model offers a robust and interpretable scheme for understanding river flow, emphasizing that while rivers are inherently dynamic and influenced by a multifaceted range of external factors, careful monitoring of these key parameters can provide valuable insights for environmental management, risk mitigation, and ecological preservation.
